source_text: Istis ergo praetermissis, accusat cur non dixerim: " cum libidine "; subditque, ut dogmatis eius acumen decebat: " Munus piorum, propagatio est fecunda filiorum, non commixtio pudenda membrorum; quam non haberet in generandis filiis natura sana, nunc autem habet eadem natura vitiata. Ac per hoc, et qui inde nascitur, indiget renasci " [n16] . Quam consequenter omnia! Munus dicit piorum, existentiam filiorum; sed hoc constituit sub diabolo, quod Deum dare confirmat, id est, filios. Libidinem autem, quae est in pudenda commixtione membrorum, diabolicam vocat; quam in parentibus esse non abnuit, quos tamen absolvit a culpa. Ex homine hunc natum dicas? Quod agunt, inquit, parentes, diabolicum est, sed rei non sunt; quod nascuntur filii, divinum opus est, sed rei sunt. Et adhuc se non Deo, sed daemoni aestimat obluctatum? Meritissime patiuntur istum furorem, qui putant esse naturale peccatum.
pass_a_gloss: These things therefore having been omitted, he accuses why I did not say: 'with lust'; and he subjoins, as the sharpness of his dogma became: 'The gift of the pious is a fertile propagation of sons, not a shameful mingling of members; which a healthy nature would not have in generating sons, but now the same nature vitiated has. And through this, even he who is born from there needs to be reborn.' How consequently all things! He says the gift of the pious is the existence of sons; but he establishes under the devil what he confirms God gives, that is, sons. But lust, which is in the shameful mingling of members, he calls diabolical; which he does not deny is in parents, whom nevertheless he acquits from fault. Would you say this one was born from a human? What the parents do, he says, is diabolical, but they are not guilty; that sons are born is a divine work, but they are guilty. And still he estimates he has struggled not against God but against the demon? Most deservedly do they suffer that fury who think there is a natural sin.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS libido; Blaise pudenda libido vs nuptiae

pass_b_english: Passing over these points, then, he accuses me of not saying ‘with lust.’ He adds, as befits his doctrine’s sharpness: ‘The fruitful production of children is a gift to the devout, not the shameful union of bodily parts. A healthy nature would not have had this in begetting children, but that same nature, now corrupted, does have it. Consequently, the one born from it needs to be reborn’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.25). How consistent it all is! He calls children’s existence a gift to the devout, but places under the devil what he affirms God gives: the children. Sexual desire, however, which is in the shameful union of bodily parts, he calls diabolical. He does not deny its presence in the parents, yet acquits them of guilt. Would you say this man was born of a human being? What the parents do, he says, is diabolical, yet they are not guilty. What the children are by being born is God’s work, yet they are guilty. And he still thinks he has fought the demon rather than God! Those who think sin is natural thoroughly deserve to suffer this madness.

choices.why: Julian's pudenda libido is the appetite accompanying union, not a created substance of sin.
Julian defends marital union (commixtio) as God's work, not the devil's property.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
